title: Somalia's Federal Supreme Court Annuls Galmudug Election Results, Orders Fresh Vote
detail: Somalia's Federal Supreme Court on Monday, August 24, 2026, annulled the results of Galmudug's July 30 combined state assembly and local council elections — the region's first direct, universal-suffrage vote — ruling that the process violated the constitution and Somalia's electoral law. Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, announcing the decision in Mogadishu, said irregularities during the vote caused 'significant damage to the independence, freedom and fairness of the elections and had affected their outcome.' The annulled results covered 63 state assembly seats (won by the Justice and Solidarity Party) plus local council races across 11 districts in the Mudug and Galgaduud regions; the Towfiiq party had challenged the results, alleging manipulation. The court ordered the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (NIEBC) to conduct a fresh election 'at the earliest possible time' following proper legal procedure, without setting a specific date; incumbent officials remain in their posts until lawfully elected replacements take office. The ruling — coming as Galmudug's vote was meant to showcase Somalia's transition toward one-person-one-vote elections, following South West State's May 2026 direct ballot — raises new doubts about that transition and adds fresh strain between Mogadishu and Galmudug's regional leadership.

media.caption: Somalia's Federal Supreme Court annulled Galmudug's July 30 election results, Aug 24, 2026
Galmudug held its first direct, universal-suffrage election on July 30, 2026, before the Supreme Court voided the results

title: Puntland Warns Ransom Payments to Somali Pirates Could Fuel Piracy's Return
detail: Puntland's Ministry of Fisheries and Marine Resources warned on Monday, August 24, 2026, that paying ransoms to pirate groups holding hijacked vessels off Somalia's coast 'could inject money and momentum into a renewed wave of attacks on vessels.' The ministry said ransom payments would give pirate groups the financial resources and incentive to continue operating and could attract new recruits into maritime criminal networks, and officials said they were tracking a rise in piracy incidents along Puntland's coastline along with preliminary evidence that outside groups were attempting to reactivate former piracy networks with financial inducements. The statement did not name a specific ransom demand or vessel but comes amid an active 2026 piracy resurgence in which at least six commercial vessels have been hijacked since April, several still held. Puntland called for sustained cooperation between local security agencies and the international maritime industry to prevent pirate networks from re-establishing a foothold along the Somali coast.

media.caption: Puntland's Ministry of Fisheries and Marine Resources warned ransom payments could fuel a renewed piracy wave, Aug 24, 2026
